study.title: Matthew 9 - Jesus Authority, Mercy and Mission
study.overview: Matthew 9 presents a sequence of signs and calls revealing who Jesus is and the kind of Kingdom he inaugurates. The chapter begins with the healing of a paralytic and the affirmation that the Son of man has authority to forgive sins. Then Jesus calls Matthew, eats with publicans and sinners, responds to criticism of fasting and shows that his presence inaugurates something new, which does not fit in the old religious manner. Then heals the daughter of a chief, a woman who had been sick for twelve years, two blind and a dumb man and demon-meal. The chapter ends with a summary of Jesus" ministry and his compassionate gaze on the crowds, which leads him to teach the disciples to pray for workers for the harvest.

outline.title: Forgiveness and healing of the paralytic
outline.explanation: Jesus enters his own city, receives the faith of the one who brings the paralytic and begins by dealing with the deepest problem: sin. By forgiving sins and then ordering man to rise up, he shows that his word has authority both to restore the relationship with God and to heal the body. The reaction of the scribes reveals opposition to their divine identity, while the multitudes respond with admiration and glorify God.

outline.title: Call Matthew, table with sinners and the new time of the Kingdom
outline.explanation: Jesus calls Matthew, a tax collector, and then sits at the table with tax collectors and sinners. To the Pharisees, he answers that he came as a doctor for the sick and cites mercy as the right meaning of God's will. On the question of fasting, Jesus teaches that his presence is like the bridegroom in the feast: there is a time of joy while he is with them, and there will be time to lament when he is taken away. The images of the new cloth and new wine teach that the reality brought about by Jesus cannot be embedded without harm in the old schemes.

outline.title: Life, healing, faith and increasing opposition
outline.explanation: A synagogue chief asks Jesus to touch his newly died daughter, and the Lord answers him with power over death. On the way, a sick woman touches her clothes in faith and is healed, showing that trust in Jesus is rewarded for her mercy. Upon arriving at the house, Jesus rebukes the uproar and resurrects the girl, and then heals two blind men who recognize him as the Son of David. Finally, he frees a dumb and demon-demon man, who leads to the crowds to amazement, but also makes the Pharisees ascribe the work of Jesus to the chief of the demons.

outline.title: Summary of ministry and call to prayer
outline.explanation: The chapter closes with an overview of Jesus" ministry: teaching in the synagogues, proclamation of the Gospel of the Kingdom and healing of all sorts of diseases. When he sees the crowds, he feels compassion because they are tired, scattered and without a shepherd. Then he declares that the harvest is great and the workers are few, calling the disciples to ask the harvest Lord to send more workers.

study.context: The text shows Jesus in his own city, identifies the presence of Pharisees, scribes and disciples of John, and also mentions publicans, sinners and flute player in an environment of mourning. The notes indicate that Matthew was also known as Levi and that the reference city in 9:1 was Capernaum. It is also indicated that grief could be public and accompanied by funeral music.
study.theology: Matthew 9 points out that Jesus not only relieves symptoms, but attacks the root of human evil: sin. His authority to forgive sins is central and sustains miracles as signs of who he is. The chapter also shows that salvation reaches people considered unclean or marginalized, such as publicans, sinners, and a ritually weakened woman, and that mercy is superior to a religiosity that isolates itself from the needy. Moreover, Jesus reveals that his presence inaugurates a new time, impossible to be restrained by ancient structures without them breaking. Finally, the chapter connects compassion and mission: Jesus sees the multitudes as sheep without a shepherd and calls his disciples to pray that God raises workers for the harvest.

scholarViews.insight: The harvest represents the multitudes, and the Lord of the harvest is God himself, whom the disciples should ask him to call more workers.
The call of Matthew shows the grace of Christ to the publicans and prepares the way to deal with their care for souls, not just by bodies.
Jesus commands the disciples to pray that God sends workers, because the impulse and qualification of service belong to the harvesting Lord.

questions: What does Jesus" command to the paralytic teach about the relationship between sin, forgiveness, and physical healing?
In what ways does the table of Jesus with publicans and sinners confront a religion based only on separation and appearance?
How can the image of the harvest guide the church today in prayer, compassion and sending of workers?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to trust in the authority of Jesus above appearances. Confess that he can forgive, restore and call who seems unlikely; receive his mercy in faith; and pray concretely so that God sends workers to the harvest, beginning with himself and by specific people of his community.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are in English and some are summarized or truncated; therefore, the synthesis here seeks to remain strictly within what was explicitly indicated. No historical, geographical or linguistic data were used that was not supported by the notes. Confessional interpretations were presented as an evangelical reading, not as absolute conclusions of the text.
